cur:objects-magdeburg-ivory-gerasene-dem.summary: Christ, followed by apostles, raises his hand toward a possessed man, while a small winged demon flees from the man's head and swine rush away at the lower right. The scene is set against a characteristic chequered openwork background, through which a gold ground once shone. It belongs to the series of small plaques that once decorated an altar or pulpit given by Otto I to his new cathedral at Magdeburg.
facts: Wikipedia notes that 16 Magdeburg Ivories survive; they were commissioned by Otto I, probably for the dedication of Magdeburg Cathedral and the raising of the see to an archbishopric in 968, for an object variously conjectured to be an antependium, throne, door or pulpit.
They are often assumed to have been made in Milan, though Peter Lasko argued for artists trained in Lorraine; the openwork backgrounds probably revealed a gilded backing.

cur:objects-pax-of-duke-ursus-cividale.summary: An ivory plaque of the Crucifixion is set in a jewelled silver frame: Christ hangs on the cross, with the Virgin and St John below and busts of the sun and moon in medallions above. Gems of red, green and blue alternate with discs of filigree around the border. Used as a 'pax', it was passed among the faithful to be kissed during Mass, so that the image of the crucified Lord became an instrument of peace.
facts: A pax (or osculatory) was a tablet offered to the clergy and congregation to kiss at the sign of peace during Mass (liturgical use).
It is traditionally associated with a Duke Ursus (Orso) of Friuli, from whom it takes its name; the museum dates it to the mid-9th century.
cur:objects-pax-of-duke-ursus-cividale.notes: The association with Duke Ursus is traditional. Some captions date it 850–900.
